source: Anderson, Bjork & Bjork (1994) Remembering can cause forgetting: retrieval dynamics in long-term memory (paradigm as described in later papers)
finding: Founding paradigm. Study category-exemplar pairs, practise some exemplars of some categories with category plus letter-stem cues, wait about 20 min, then test everything. Practised items (Rp+) are recalled better. Unpractised items from practised categories (Rp-) are recalled worse than items from unpractised categories (Nrp). That gap is retrieval-induced forgetting (RIF). Explained by inhibition of competing items during practice.
numbers: Original 1994 numbers not opened this session. Replication paper cites Exp 2 of the original as n=36 and says the original effect size could not be computed from the paper (insufficient data).
limits: I read the paradigm as described in secondary sources, not the 1994 PDF (PDF fetch blocked, HTTP 429).
agent_relevance: Warning for the agent: practising or retrieving one item of a related set can lower later access to its siblings. Design rule: do not repeatedly rehearse one lesson inside a set of sibling lessons without a check on the siblings.

source: Wikipedia (2025) Retrieval-induced forgetting (tertiary overview of paradigm details)
finding: Typical design: 48 items in 8 categories of 6. Anderson 1994 used 30 s per category cue (about 5 s per item). RIF = Nrp minus Rp-. Final tests can be category-cued, category plus stem, or recognition. RIF generalises to homographs, locations, propositions, mock crime scenes and personality traits.
numbers: Goodmon & Anderson (2011) Exp 1 as cited: Rp+ 81%, Nrp 68%, Rp- 55% (13-point RIF). Restudy instead of retrieval gives no RIF. Extra-list or impossible practice still gives RIF. Group conversation gives socially shared RIF.
limits: Tertiary source; numbers come from the page, not from the primary papers. Page read to character 100000 of 105911.
agent_relevance: Shows RIF is not only a word-list artefact. Any scaffold that stores related items and re-retrieves one could show it.

source: Rowland, Bates & DeLosh (2014) On the reliability of retrieval-induced forgetting. Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Direct replication of Anderson 1994 Exp 1 with undergraduates (Exp 1, N=72) and an internet sample (Exp 2, N=140). RIF replicated both times. The independent-cue procedure of Anderson and Spellman 1995 (Exp 3, N=67) did not replicate.
numbers: Exp 1: Nrp 0.45 vs Rp- 0.41, t(71)=2.59, p=.01, d=0.31; Rp+ 0.79. Exp 2: Nrp 0.50 vs Rp- 0.42, t(139)=4.51, d=0.38; Rp+ 0.63. Exp 3: Rp- 0.56 vs Nrp-similar 0.52, t(66)=0.92, p=.36; cue-independent RIF d=-0.05, 95% CI (-0.36, 0.27). Power plan: 70 people for d=0.4 at power .95.
quote: Retrieval-induced forgetting was observed when using the traditional retrieval practice paradigm
limits: Effect is small (d about 0.3 to 0.4). The cue-independent form, the key inhibition evidence, was an uninformative failure under the Simonsohn 2014 test (CI includes both 0 and d33%=0.21).
agent_relevance: Plan for a small but real cost. Do not rely on the cue-independent form of the effect.

source: Rowland et al. (2014), small-telescopes benchmarks for the originals
finding: Replication uses Simonsohn's small-telescopes test. The original Anderson 1994 Exp 2 (n=36) could only detect d33%=0.26. Original Anderson and Spellman 1995 Exp 2 (n=54) had d33%=0.21.
numbers: d33% 0.26 (n=36) and 0.21 (n=54). Replications d=0.31 and 0.38 exceed 0.26.
limits: Shows the original studies were small, so original effect sizes are probably inflated.
agent_relevance: Treat published RIF magnitudes as upper bounds when setting thresholds for sibling-damage checks.

source: Raaijmakers & Jakab (2012) Retrieval-induced forgetting without competition: testing the retrieval specificity assumption of the inhibition theory. Memory & Cognition
finding: Anderson, Bjork & Bjork (2000) found RIF only when practice needed competitive retrieval (recall the item from its category) and not when the category was recalled from the item. Raaijmakers and Jakab ran the noncompetitive version (recall the category name) and still found RIF. This conflicts with the retrieval-specificity claim of inhibition theory and fits strength-based competition (SAM).
numbers: Exp 1 (N=24): Rp+ 64%, Nrp 44%, Rp- 38%; RIF F(1,22)=7.29, p=.013, eta2p=.233. Exp 2 (N=24, type only the category name): Rp+ 61%, Nrp 47%, Rp- 41%, F(1,12)=6.51, p=.025. Category recall in practice 98.5% and 99%. RIF was 10% for first-tested and 2% for later-tested items in Exp 1.
limits: Small samples. Authors argue Anderson 2000 had no feedback in practice, giving bimodal strength; the noncompetitive task there may have strengthened less. Not a refutation of inhibition in other paradigms.
agent_relevance: A noninhibitory story (stronger siblings win cue competition) predicts the same sibling damage. A guard must work whichever mechanism is true.

source: Raaijmakers (2016) On testing the strength independence assumption in retrieval-induced forgetting. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review
finding: Strength independence says the gain in practised items should not correlate with the loss in Rp- items; no correlation was taken as evidence for inhibition. Simulations of a simplified SAM model (no inhibition) show that SAM also predicts a near-zero between-subject correlation. So the correlation test cannot separate the theories.
numbers: 10,000 simulated experiments with 32 subjects each. Mean practised-item accuracy .738. Final recall: Rp+ .769, Rp- .539, Nrp .641 (practice effect 12.8%, RIF 10.2%). Mean correlation r=.020, SD .181; only 6.4% of experiments significant (one-sided).
limits: Simulation, not behavioural data. Murayama 2014 found a positive across-study correlation, but Raaijmakers says that analysis mixed output-interference conditions and ran across experiments.
agent_relevance: Key formal model: SAM with strengthening only. It reproduces RIF with no suppression. A cheap implementation test: simulate sibling strengths in the agent memory and see whether sibling loss follows from strength gaps alone.

source: Raaijmakers (2016), SAM explanation of the restudy dissociation
finding: Standard result: restudy gives the same Rp+ gain as retrieval but no RIF. Raaijmakers and Jakab (2012) showed a noninhibitory strength model reproduces this if only retrieved items are strengthened and successful retrieval strengthens much more than a study trial.
numbers: Qualitative; model parameters not recorded.
limits: The model assumption (retrieval strengthens more than restudy) is itself untested here.
agent_relevance: Retrieval, not mere re-reading, is the risky act. Re-reading a lesson in the prompt is likely less harmful to siblings than quizzing on it.

source: Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli & Storm (2014) Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: a meta-analytic review of retrieval-induced forgetting. Psychological Bulletin
finding: First major meta-analysis of RIF. Results largely support inhibition accounts but give some challenging evidence, with outcomes varying by how RIF was assessed (test type, output-interference control).
numbers: Abstract only; no effect sizes captured.
limits: Abstract-level; full text paywalled. Raaijmakers 2016 criticises its correlation analysis.
agent_relevance: Headline reference for RIF robustness; pull numbers from the full text in a later pass.

source: Anderson & Green (2001) Suppressing unwanted memories by executive control. Nature
finding: Think/no-think task. Repeatedly avoiding a memory when its cue appears makes it harder to recall later. Forgetting grows with the number of suppression attempts, resists incentives for accurate recall, and is caused by processes that suppress the memory itself.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only. Related but distinct from RIF: suppression, not selective retrieval.
agent_relevance: A sibling mechanism: actively stopping a thought also lowers later access. Matters for any operator that says stop thinking about the wrong idea.

source: Anderson & Hanslmayr (2014) Neural mechanisms of motivated forgetting. Trends in Cognitive Sciences
finding: Review: suppressing awareness of an unwelcome memory is achieved by inhibitory control from lateral prefrontal cortex, which also disrupts traces that support retention. Cue independence (forgetting persists with a different test cue) is taken as strong evidence for inhibition of the trace itself. Forgetting also appears on recognition and indirect priming tests. Socially shared RIF: listeners forget details a speaker omits.
numbers: Qualitative review; example: suppress 'roach' from cue 'ordeal' and recall is worse with test cue 'Insect' too.
limits: Authors are leading inhibition proponents; the competing review by Raaijmakers and Jakab 2013 was not opened.
agent_relevance: Provides the inhibition account list of signatures to test in an agent (cue independence, graded by repetition).

source: Wimber, Alink, Charest, Kriegeskorte & Anderson (2015) Retrieval induces adaptive forgetting of competing memories via cortical pattern suppression. Nature Neuroscience
finding: fMRI pattern tracking showed that repeatedly retrieving a target suppressed the cortical pattern unique to the competitor over four retrieval repetitions. Suppression engaged mid-ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and predicted later forgetting of that competitor.
numbers: N=24 (20 female). Each target retrieved 4 times. Recognition of competitors 75.2% vs baseline 82.1%, t(23)=4.91; interaction F(1,23)=4.70, p=.041. Prefrontal activity decrease predicted competitor suppression slope: left IFG R=-0.65, p<.001; right IFG R=-0.48, p=.009; no relation to target up-regulation (left IFG R=0.25, ns).
limits: Small N. One-tailed tests for directional hypotheses. Picture-pair materials, recognition test.
agent_relevance: First direct neural evidence of competitor suppression as it happens. Competition shows as intrusions early, then fades as the loser is demoted.

source: Khan, Ti, Yuan, Crespo Garcia, Anderson & Tong (2024) Medial prefrontal cortex stimulation reduces retrieval-induced forgetting via fronto-parietal beta desynchronization. J Neuroscience
finding: Anodal tDCS over mPFC before retrieval practice reduced RIF but left target retrieval unchanged: forgetting is a side effect that can be separated from strengthening of the target. Reduced RIF came with stronger left-DLPFC beta desynchronisation (<500 ms).
numbers: N=50 (25 stim, 25 sham). Across groups NRP- 69.42% vs RP- 59.82%, F(1,48)=78.82, p<.001. Group x item type F(1,48)=9.07, p=.004. RIF stimulation 6.25% (SD 7.36) vs sham 12.83% (SD 7.81). RIF significant in both (t(24)=4.25 and 8.22).
limits: Single stimulation protocol, one lab; no beta-RIF correlation in the sham group.
agent_relevance: Evidence that target gain and sibling loss are separable. Supports a separate guard for siblings rather than weaker retrieval.

source: Racsmany & Keresztes (2015) Initial retrieval shields against retrieval-induced forgetting. Frontiers in Psychology
finding: RIF appeared only when practice was retesting (not restudy) on a delayed final test. When participants first retrieved the whole learning set before selective retrieval, selective practice caused no drop in related items. Authors read this as support for a context-shift account of RIF.
numbers: Exp 1: retest RIF t(28)=-3.13, p=.004, r=.37; restudy no RIF t(29)=1.43, p=.16. Practised-item gain: t(28)=5.91, r=.60 (restudy), t(29)=9.94, r=.70 (retest). Post hoc power 0.88. Exp 2 N=30 (within-subject retest vs restudy, initial retrieval first): no decrease in related items.
limits: Hungarian students, small samples; Exp 4 replicates with an Nrp baseline. Inhibition not ruled out by this alone.
agent_relevance: Practical protective move: recall the whole set once before drilling a subset. Touch every sibling before practising one.

source: Spitzer (2014) Finding retrieval-induced forgetting in recognition tests: a case for baseline memory strength. Frontiers in Psychology
finding: In recognition tests, absence of RIF can be predicted from very low baseline memory strength. RIF acts as a proportional impairment of any process contributing to recognition. Strengthening of practised items does not predict the size of RIF.
numbers: Survey of recognition-RIF studies; no new experiment; no per-study figures recorded.
limits: Review; I read the abstract and opening only.
agent_relevance: A weak sibling cannot be seen to be damaged. Use sensitive tests and strong baselines before claiming no damage.

source: Overview boundary list: Verde & Perfect (2011), Dodd et al. (2006), Jakab & Raaijmakers (2009), Goodmon & Anderson (2011), Storm et al. (2006) as summarised on Wikipedia
finding: Boundary conditions: recognition RIF absent under time pressure; practice in the same order as study reduces RIF; item strength matters; semantic integration of items reduces RIF; retrieval success not needed for RIF (impossible practice still gives it).
numbers: Impossible retrieval practice still gives RIF (qualitative).
limits: Second-hand list; primary papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Integration of siblings into one structure may protect them: link lessons rather than store them as isolated items.

source: Norman, Newman & Detre (2007) A neural network model of retrieval-induced forgetting. Psychological Review
finding: Neural network learning rule using oscillating feedback inhibition: it strengthens weak parts of target memories and weakens competing memories. It accounts for why practice causes more forgetting than presenting the target, effects of competitor and target strength, and why RIF sometimes generalises to independent cues and sometimes does not.
numbers: Abstract only; simulation numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Main computational model of the inhibition account. Weakening may hit only moderately active competitors, so very weak or very strong siblings might be spared.

source: Midler & McClelland (2023) Retrieval induced forgetting in a non-monotonic hippocampal model (bioRxiv preprint)
finding: Replicates Ritvo et al. (2023): a hippocampus-like network with U-shaped (non-monotonic) plasticity produces RIF and pulls competitor representations apart. A monotonic baseline failed. The model fails to produce reverse RIF (relearning forgotten items).
numbers: Moderate input pushes weights down; high input pushes up; threshold at percentile rank 0.6 of hidden-unit stimulation. Each hidden unit connects to 50% of input units. No effect sizes in the parts read.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed; model fails the reverse-RIF test.
agent_relevance: Shows RIF can emerge from a learning rule alone, with no explicit controller. Relevant if an LLM fine-tuned on one fact shows damage to neighbours.

source: Kovacs & Harris (2022) Retrieval-induced forgetting with novel visual stimuli is retrieval-specific and strength-independent. Memory
finding: Graded measure with novel shapes drawn from memory. RIF in retrieval practice, none in a copying (restudy) condition despite large gains for practised items, and no sign of strength dependence.
limits: Abstract only. Supports inhibition, opposing Raaijmakers and Jakab (2012).
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to strength-only models; keep both explanations alive in design.

source: Pica, Chernikova, Pierro et al. (2018) Retrieval-induced forgetting as motivated cognition. Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Review: RIF magnitude depends on motivation. High need for closure (NFC) increases RIF, except when the forgotten information serves the retriever goals. Self-threat modulates RIF.
numbers: Three witness-scenario studies: high-NFC participants showed larger RIF in free recall (Study 1), with letter cues controlling output interference (Study 2), and in a two-burglary scenario (Study 3). Effect sizes not captured.
limits: Review of a small set of studies by overlapping authors.
agent_relevance: Wanting a quick answer increases forgetting of alternatives. An agent pushed to close may suppress alternatives more.

source: Cinel, Cortis Mack & Ward (2018) Towards augmented human memory: retrieval-induced forgetting and retrieval practice in an interactive, end-of-day review. J Exp Psychol: General
finding: RIF appears in real campus-tour and scavenger-hunt memory, not just lab word lists. Practising some objects from a location raised their recall and lowered unpractised objects from the same location (Exp 1, replicated in Exp 2). Exps 3 to 6 tuned retrieval schedules to maximise or minimise recall of chosen items.
numbers: Six experiments. Exp 1 used a campus tour with category-cued free recall after a filled delay. Effect sizes not captured.
limits: Field-like stimuli; sizes not read in detail.
agent_relevance: RIF can be used on purpose: schedule retrieval to promote chosen items. Also a hazard: end-of-day review may trade siblings for targets.

source: Matsumoto, Mochizuki, Marsh & Kawaguchi (2021) Repeated retrieval of generalized memories can impair specific autobiographical recall: a retrieval induced forgetting account. J Exp Psychol: General
finding: Repeatedly retrieving general autobiographical memories lowered recall of specific ones. Effect was cue independent in Exp 2 and larger under high competition than low competition (Exp 3).
numbers: Three experiments; exact statistics not captured.
limits: Autobiographical, self-generated stimuli.
agent_relevance: Broad, generic recall can crowd out specific details. In an agent, repeated summarising may erase specifics.

source: Mall & Morey (2013) High working memory capacity predicts less retrieval induced forgetting. PLoS ONE
finding: Low working memory capacity people had more RIF and no retrieval benefit when interference demands were high. High-capacity people showed RIF between categories but not within overlapping categories.
numbers: Practice recall of overlapping items 28.6% vs distinct 51.2% in the lowest-WMC group (p<.0001); highest-WMC 44.0% vs 43.2% (p=.84). Distinct vs overlap overall 45.5% vs 34.1%, F(1,122)=22.23, p<.001.
limits: Qualifies, not refutes, inhibition: adds a focused-search account.
agent_relevance: Smaller effective working space may mean more sibling damage when items overlap.

source: Noreen & MacLeod (2015) What do we really know about cognitive inhibition? Task demands and inhibitory effects across a range of memory and behavioural tasks. PLoS ONE
finding: 87 participants did RIF, think/no-think, Stroop and Go/No-Go. Forgetting appeared in both memory tasks but did not correlate with each other or with behavioural inhibition. Questions a single general inhibition process.
numbers: TNT same-probe: respond 91.76% vs baseline 83.24%, d=0.55; no-think 74.90%, d=1.02. Independent probe: no-think 70.21% vs baseline 80.17%, t(86)=3.60, d=0.55. Impossible-practice RIF: Rp- 68.65% vs Nrp 77.94%, F(1,85)=21.90, d=0.66; about 8% (possible) and 10% (impossible).
limits: One sample, N=87; low cross-task correlation may reflect poor reliability.
agent_relevance: Do not assume one inhibition knob. Sibling controls must be tested per task.

source: Loftus (2005) Planting misinformation in the human mind: a 30-year investigation of the malleability of memory. Learning & Memory
finding: Review of the misinformation effect: impairment of memory after misleading post-event information. Susceptibility conditions, warnings that sometimes work, observation in other species, group differences, fate of the original trace, and implanting false memories of rich events.
numbers: Abstract only; Loftus and Palmer 1974 speed estimates not opened.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: The second memory-error route: new text competes with or replaces old. In an agent, a wrong hint in context can displace earlier correct content.

source: Wikipedia (2025): clinical groups in RIF (ADHD, depression, schizophrenia)
finding: ADHD: controls similar on category-cued tests, less RIF on category-plus-stem. Depression: no RIF on category-plus-stem (Potts et al. 2012). Schizophrenia: comparable on category-cued, reduced on recognition.
numbers: No numbers in the page text.
limits: Tertiary summary.
agent_relevance: RIF depends on executive resources; a degraded control process changes the effect.

source: Camp et al. (2007) and Aslan et al. (2007), as summarised on Wikipedia
finding: Item-specific independent cues produced no RIF, argued to count against a general inhibition account. Older adults showed no inhibitory deficit.
numbers: Not given.
limits: Second-hand; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Weakens the claim that siblings are inhibited rather than blocked by cue competition.

source: Anderson & Spellman (1995) cue-independence logic, tested by Rowland et al. (2014) Exp 3
finding: Cue-independent RIF: related items from other categories sharing an implicit link are also impaired. Seen as strong support for inhibition because the test cue differs. Rowland attempt found no effect.
numbers: Rowland Exp 3 (N=67): related-condition NRP-similar 0.50 vs unrelated 0.52, t(66)=0.39, p=.7. Original Exp 2 n=54.
limits: Single failed replication in the uninformative range; not a disproof.
agent_relevance: The agent may not need to guard cross-category damage as heavily as within-set damage.
